sheet.howExamined: M4 (Higher, calculator, 2 hours, 100 marks, 21–24 questions). A bounds item in 14 of the 15 M4 papers from Summer 2018 to Summer 2026 (none in Summer 2022), usually at Q12–Q17: a bare difference (Summer 2018 Q12, Summer 2019 Q15), a quotient or a speed (January 2019 Q15, January 2020 Q23, Summer 2021 Q14, November 2021 Q21 with the answer in hours and minutes, November 2023 Q20), a formula rearranged (November 2022 Q14, W = Fd, both bounds). Three marks when the bounds go into a printed formula: Summer 2024 Q16 (h = u² ÷ 2a, answer 23.36456538), November 2024 Q16 (S = V² ÷ 2g, answer 10.35504844), Summer 2026 Q14 (F = ma, minimum acceleration, answer in m/s²). Four marks when a second stage is added: Summer 2023 Q15 (maximum average speed from 62 km and 1 hour 11 minutes, answer 53.19148936), Summer 2025 Q13 (greatest number of containers from masses to the nearest 5 kg and the nearest 100 kg, answer 32), November 2025 Q17 (upper bound of the third side of a right-angled triangle, answer 3.863512003). The schemes are MA1 chains — one mark for the bounds identified, one for the substitution, an A1 for the value — and the value printed in the scheme is the full display, so a rounded answer risks the A mark unless the question states an accuracy. Command words: Calculate, Find, Work out, Write down, with greatest possible, least possible, maximum and minimum doing the work in the stem.
traps: Halving the wrong thing: 50 kg to the nearest 5 kg has bounds 47.5 and 52.5, not 45 and 55 — the single commonest loss on this topic (Summer 2025 M4 Q13)
Leaving a count of whole objects as a decimal, or rounding it up: a greatest possible number of items rounds down (Summer 2025 M4 Q13)
Bounding the answer instead of the inputs: calculating with the given values and then adding a half unit to the result (November 2025 M4 Q17, where about 30% scored full marks)

Treating 1 hour 11 minutes as 1.11 hours, or bounding 71 minutes and then forgetting to divide by 60 (Summer 2023 M4 Q15)

noteBlocks.lede: A measurement is never exact. A crate weighed as 50 kg to the nearest 5 kg could be anything from 47.5 kg up to 52.5 kg. Put two numbers like that into a subtraction or a division and the answer drifts too: this topic finds how far, in each direction.
can: Write both bounds of any rounded value from its half unit.
Pair an upper bound with a lower one for the greatest or least difference or quotient.
Carry bounds through a speed, a printed formula, a count or Pythagoras.

noteBlocks.text: A rounded value is an interval

noteBlocks.md: A value given **correct to** some accuracy stands for every value that rounds to it. The distance from the stated value to either end of that interval is the **half unit**: half of the rounding unit. So 50 kg to the nearest 5 kg runs from 47.5 kg up to 52.5 kg, and the upper end is never quite reached.

Read the rounding unit from the question's own words: nearest 10 m, one decimal place, three significant figures. For significant figures, find the column of the last significant figure first; one of that column is the rounding unit.

noteBlocks.stem: Write down the lower and upper bounds of: $80$ m to the nearest $10$ m; $3.7$ kg to $1$ decimal place; $62\,400$ people to $3$ significant figures.

steps.decision: The rounding unit is 10 m, so the half unit is 5 m either side.
One decimal place means the nearest 0.1, so the half unit is 0.05.
The third significant figure, 4, is in the hundreds column, so the rounding unit is 100 and the half unit 50.

noteBlocks.prompt: A bag of sand is $25$ kg, correct to the nearest kilogram. What is the half unit?
noteBlocks.explain: Nearest kilogram makes the rounding unit 1 kg, and the half unit is half of it, as each step of See it halved its own unit: 0.5 kg. So the bag is anywhere from 24.5 kg up to 25.5 kg.

optionNotes.why: 1 kg is the rounding unit itself. The bounds sit half a unit either side, so the half unit is 0.5 kg.
25 kg is the measurement, not its accuracy. The accuracy is the nearest kilogram, and half of 1 kg is 0.5 kg.

twin.prompt: A plank is $240$ cm, correct to the nearest $10$ cm. What is the half unit?
twin.explain: Nearest 10 cm makes the rounding unit 10 cm, and the half unit is half of it: 5 cm, so the plank is from 235 cm up to 245 cm.

optionNotes.why: 10 cm is the rounding unit. Half of it, 5 cm, sits either side of 240 cm.
That halves 1 cm, but the plank is measured to the nearest 10 cm, so the half unit is half of 10: 5 cm.

noteBlocks.prompt: A rod is $0.582$ m long, correct to $3$ significant figures. Its lower bound, in metres, is
noteBlocks.explain: The last significant figure, 2, is in the thousandths, so the rounding unit is 0.001 and the half unit 0.0005, as step 3 of See it found the column first: 0.582 − 0.0005 = 0.5815.

twin.prompt: A pipe is $7.36$ m long, correct to $3$ significant figures. Its upper bound, in metres, is
twin.explain: The 6 is in the hundredths, so the half unit is 0.005: 7.36 + 0.005 = 7.365.

noteBlocks.caption: The greatest gap runs between the far ends of the two bands, the least between the near ends.

noteBlocks.md: In $a - b$ the $b$ is taken away, and taking away less leaves more. So the greatest difference uses the largest $a$ with the smallest $b$, and the least difference the smallest $a$ with the largest $b$: on the number line, the far ends and the near ends.

noteBlocks.title: Division works against its bottom number
noteBlocks.md: Dividing by a smaller number gives a bigger answer, so a quotient crosses over in the same way: the greatest $a \div b$ is $\text{UB}(a) \div \text{LB}(b)$. Addition and multiplication never cross over, which is why a sum or a product pairs upper with upper.

noteBlocks.stem: $a = 9$ and $b = 4$, each correct to the nearest whole number. Try every pairing of the bounds in $a - b$.

steps.decision: Half of 1 either side of each value.
Far ends give the widest gap, near ends the narrowest: the largest a with the smallest b, then the reverse.
Two uppers or two lowers land in between, so neither is a bound of the difference.

noteBlocks.prompt: To make $a \div b$ as **small** as possible you use
options: the lower bound of a and the upper bound of b
the lower bound of a and the lower bound of b
the upper bound of a and the lower bound of b
noteBlocks.answer: the lower bound of a and the upper bound of b
noteBlocks.explain: A division works against its bottom number, as the subtraction in See it worked against b: a bigger b makes a ÷ b smaller. So the least quotient takes the smallest a over the largest b.

optionNotes.option: the lower bound of a and the lower bound of b
optionNotes.why: A smaller b makes the quotient bigger, not smaller. For the least a ÷ b the bottom must be as large as possible: the upper bound of b.

optionNotes.option: the upper bound of a and the lower bound of b
optionNotes.why: That pairing makes the largest quotient: the biggest top over the smallest bottom. The least quotient is the reverse.

twin.prompt: To make $p \div q$ as **large** as possible you use
options: the upper bound of p and the lower bound of q
the upper bound of p and the upper bound of q
the lower bound of p and the upper bound of q
twin.answer: the upper bound of p and the lower bound of q
twin.explain: The largest quotient puts the biggest top over the smallest bottom, because dividing by less gives more.

optionNotes.option: the upper bound of p and the upper bound of q
optionNotes.why: A larger q makes p ÷ q smaller, so two uppers fall short of the greatest value. Pair the upper bound of p with the lower bound of q.

optionNotes.option: the lower bound of p and the upper bound of q
optionNotes.why: That pairing gives the least quotient: the smallest top over the largest bottom.

noteBlocks.text: A difference: the greatest and the least

noteBlocks.md: An exam item gives each value with its own accuracy, often different ones. Write all four bounds first, then choose the pair: the greatest $a - b$ is $\text{UB}(a) - \text{LB}(b)$ and the least is $\text{LB}(a) - \text{UB}(b)$. The bounds are usually the first mark, so they belong on the page before any subtraction.
The specification's own example is a circle cut from a rectangle of paper. The paper left is a difference of two areas, so its greatest value takes the largest rectangle and the smallest circle.

noteBlocks.stem: A circle of radius $4.2$ cm is cut from a rectangle of card $15.6$ cm by $10.3$ cm. Each measurement is correct to $1$ decimal place. Calculate the greatest possible area of card left.

steps.decision: Largest card: both sides at their upper bounds. Smallest circle: the radius at its lower bound, because the circle is taken away.
The rectangle's area is a product, so upper times upper.
The circle's area from the smallest radius.
Largest minus smallest gives the greatest area left. Leave the display unless an accuracy is asked.

noteBlocks.prompt: $a = 7.6$ and $b = 3.2$, each correct to $1$ d.p. The greatest possible value of $a - b$ is
noteBlocks.explain: The greatest difference takes the largest a and the smallest b, as step 1 of See it took the largest card and the smallest circle: 7.65 − 3.15 = 4.5.

noteBlocks.md: Speed $=$ distance $\div$ time and density $=$ mass $\div$ volume are quotients, and neither is on the Higher formula sheet. The greatest speed takes the longest distance over the shortest time; the least speed, the shortest distance over the longest time. Write both bounds of each quantity before you divide.

noteBlocks.stem: A cyclist covers $750$ m, correct to the nearest $10$ m, in $68.4$ s, correct to $1$ decimal place. Find the upper bound of the average speed.

steps.decision: Half of 10 m and half of 0.1 s. The largest speed wants the longest distance and the shortest time.
Upper over lower: dividing by the smaller time gives the larger speed.
Leave the full display: the scheme prints the long value.

noteBlocks.title: Solving Limits of Accuracy Problems
noteBlocks.why: The same pairings at writing speed on more problems, divisions included. Watch it once, then answer the check without going back.

noteBlocks.prompt: A trolley rolls $84$ cm, correct to the nearest cm, in $3.5$ s, correct to $1$ d.p. Its least possible average speed, in cm/s, to $3$ d.p., is
noteBlocks.explain: The least speed takes the shortest distance over the longest time, the reverse of See it's pairing: 83.5 ÷ 3.55 = 23.521 to 3 d.p.

twin.prompt: A tank fills with $450$ litres, correct to the nearest $10$ litres, in $12.6$ minutes, correct to $1$ d.p. Its greatest possible rate, in litres per minute, to $3$ d.p., is
twin.explain: The greatest rate takes the most water over the shortest time: 455 ÷ 12.55 = 36.255 to 3 d.p.

noteBlocks.md: CCEA usually prints the formula and asks for one bound. Read it symbol by symbol: a letter on the top takes the bound in the direction you want, a letter on the bottom the opposite one, and a letter after a minus sign works against the answer too. Numbers in the formula, such as the 2 in $2a$, are exact.

noteBlocks.title: Where the 2024 formula marks went
noteBlocks.md: Both 2024 papers put bounds into a formula with a square on top and a doubled letter underneath. The reports say most candidates found the bounds; the slips named were a top letter not squared, a bottom letter not doubled, and a rounded final display.

noteBlocks.stem: $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$, where $v = 24.6$, $u = 8.3$ and $t = 3.2$, each correct to $1$ decimal place. Find the upper bound of $a$.

steps.decision: Largest a: the top as large as possible, so the largest v minus the smallest u, over the smallest t.
Substitute once, with every bound in place before any arithmetic.
The top first: the subtraction inside it follows the difference rule.
Leave the full display; round only if the question names an accuracy.

noteBlocks.prompt: $h = \dfrac{u^2}{2a}$ with $u = 4.2$ and $a = 2.5$, each to $1$ d.p. The upper bound of $h$, to $3$ d.p., is
noteBlocks.explain: u is on the top, so take its upper bound and square it; a is on the bottom, so take its lower bound and double it, as See it chose each letter: 4.25² ÷ (2 × 2.45) = 3.686 to 3 d.p.

twin.prompt: $h = \dfrac{u^2}{2a}$ with $u = 6.8$ and $a = 3.4$, each to $1$ d.p. The lower bound of $h$, to $3$ d.p., is
twin.explain: Lower bound: the smallest u on top, the largest a underneath: 6.75² ÷ (2 × 3.45) = 6.603 to 3 d.p.

noteBlocks.md: A greatest possible number of whole items is a division: the largest total over the smallest single item. Then round **down**. The next item would go over even the largest allowed total, so a decimal, or a count rounded up, is not a possible answer.

noteBlocks.stem: Boxes each have a mass of $12$ kg, correct to the nearest kg. A lift can carry $450$ kg, correct to the nearest $10$ kg. Work out the greatest possible number of boxes the lift can carry.

steps.decision: Half of 1 kg and half of 10 kg. The most boxes come from the lightest box and the largest load.
Largest load over lightest box.
A 40th box would take the load past 455 kg even at 11.5 kg each, so round down.

noteBlocks.prompt: A greatest possible number of crates works out as $17.92$. What goes on the answer line?
noteBlocks.explain: Only whole crates count, and an 18th would go over even the largest allowed load, so a greatest count rounds down, as step 3 of See it did: 17.

twin.prompt: A greatest possible number of tiles works out as $41.97$. What goes on the answer line?
twin.explain: A 42nd tile would not fit within any allowed total, so round down: 41.

noteBlocks.md: **A time in hours and minutes** (Summer 2023). Change the whole time to minutes, bound it, then divide by 60. Writing 1 h 10.5 min as 1.105 h, one of the commonest slips that year, treats minutes as hundredths of an hour.
**An answer in hours and minutes** (November 2021). A least time is the shortest distance over the greatest speed; then turn the decimal part of the hours into minutes by multiplying it by 60.
**A formula to rearrange** (November 2022, Summer 2026). $W = Fd$ asked for the force, $F = ma$ for the acceleration: rearrange first, then choose each bound by where its letter sits.

**Mixed accuracies** (November 2022, Summer 2025, Summer 2026). Nearest 5 kg beside nearest 100 kg, or nearest metre beside 3 significant figures: each value gets its own half unit. In Summer 2025 more candidates used 45 kg than 47.5 kg for 50 kg to the nearest 5 kg.
**Both bounds asked** (January 2019, November 2022). The least and the greatest in one question: write the four bounds once and use them twice, crossing over for each.

noteBlocks.md: November 2025 asked for the upper bound of a shorter side of a right-angled triangle, and about 30% scored full marks. The shorter side squared is the hypotenuse squared minus the other side squared: a subtraction, so the upper bound takes the largest hypotenuse and the smallest known side. Bound the inputs, never the answer.

noteBlocks.title: Where this specification stops
noteBlocks.md: CCEA asks for a greatest, a least or a named bound as a value. Error-interval notation such as $47.5 \le m < 52.5$, percentage error and truncated readings appear in no M4 bounds question. Bounds of a sum or a product alone belong to M3.

noteBlocks.stem: In triangle $PQR$ the angle at $Q$ is a right angle. $PR = 15.2$ cm and $PQ = 9.7$ cm, each correct to $1$ decimal place. Find the upper bound of $QR$.

steps.decision: PQ is subtracted inside Pythagoras, so its smallest value leaves the largest QR.
Square each bound, then subtract.
Root last, and leave the display: a rounded root risks the accuracy mark.

noteBlocks.prompt: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse $10.4$ cm and one shorter side $6.1$ cm, each correct to $1$ d.p. Which gives the **lower** bound of the third side?
noteBlocks.explain: The least third side reverses See it's pairing: the smallest hypotenuse, minus the largest known side, because taking away more leaves less: √(10.35² − 6.15²).

optionNotes.why: 6.05 is the smallest known side, and taking away less leaves more. For a lower bound take away the largest, 6.15.
That bounds the answer, not the inputs. A half unit does not survive squaring and a square root: bound 10.4 and 6.1 first.

twin.prompt: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse $13.6$ cm and one shorter side $8.2$ cm, each correct to $1$ d.p. Which gives the **upper** bound of the third side?
twin.explain: The largest hypotenuse and the smallest known side: taking away less leaves more.

optionNotes.why: Two upper bounds: the larger side takes away more, so this falls short of the greatest. Use the lower bound, 8.15.
That bounds the answer. Bound 13.6 and 8.2 first, then calculate once.

noteBlocks.md: A question may ask for a value to a **suitable degree of accuracy**. Round both bounds to 1, then 2, then 3 significant figures, and stop at the last accuracy where they agree: those are the figures you know. No CCEA M4 paper has set it yet; it tests whether the bounds mean something to you.

noteBlocks.stem: A speed has lower bound $4.9861\ldots$ m/s and upper bound $5.0273\ldots$ m/s. Give the speed to a suitable degree of accuracy.

steps.decision: They agree, so the first figure is known.
Still the same: two figures are known.
Now they differ, so the third figure is not known.

noteBlocks.finalAnswer: $5.0$ m/s: both bounds round to $5.0$ to $2$ s.f. and differ at $3$ s.f.

noteBlocks.prompt: A length has bounds $8.4713\ldots$ m and $8.4749\ldots$ m. To a suitable degree of accuracy it is
noteBlocks.explain: Round both bounds, as See it did: to 3 significant figures both give 8.47, but to 4 they give 8.471 and 8.475, which differ. So 8.47 m is the accuracy both bounds support.

optionNotes.why: At 4 significant figures the bounds give 8.471 and 8.475, which differ, so the fourth figure is not known. Stop at 8.47 m.
A midpoint is not an accuracy. Round both bounds and keep only the figures they share: 8.47 m.

twin.explain: Both bounds give 12.4 to 3 significant figures; to 4 they give 12.36 and 12.40, which differ.

optionNotes.why: At 4 significant figures the bounds give 12.36 and 12.40, so the fourth figure is not known.

noteBlocks.text: Where the half unit comes from

noteBlocks.md: Why half? A value rounds to 50 to the nearest 5 when 50 is the closest multiple of 5 to it. The neighbouring multiples are 45 and 55, and the choice switches halfway to each of them. Halfway is always half the rounding unit from the stated value, whatever the unit.

noteBlocks.stem: Show that a value of $50$ to the nearest $5$ has bounds $47.5$ and $52.5$.

steps.decision: Rounding to the nearest 5 picks the closest multiple of 5.
At each halfway point the closest multiple changes, so these are the ends of the interval.
Each end is half the rounding unit from 50: the half unit, for any unit.

noteBlocks.finalAnswer: Bounds $= 50 \pm \tfrac{5}{2}$: the stated value plus or minus half the rounding unit

noteBlocks.prompt: A field is $300$ m long, correct to the nearest $20$ m. What is the lower bound of its length?
noteBlocks.explain: The neighbours of 300 in steps of 20 are 280 and 320, and the switch to 280 happens halfway, at 290, as See it found 47.5 halfway between 45 and 50. So 290 m.

optionNotes.why: 280 m is the neighbouring multiple of 20, but the switch happens halfway to it, at 290 m.
That halves 1 m, but the length is to the nearest 20 m. Half of 20 is 10, so 290 m.

twin.prompt: A crowd is $4000$, correct to the nearest $500$. What is the upper bound?
twin.explain: The neighbours are 3500 and 4500; the switch to 4500 happens halfway, at 4250.

optionNotes.why: 4500 is the next multiple of 500. The switch to it happens halfway, at 4250.
That halves 1, but the crowd is to the nearest 500. Half of 500 is 250, so 4250.

noteBlocks.md:
Turn any stated accuracy into a half unit, then both bounds.
Pair an upper with a lower for the greatest or least difference or quotient.
Put bounds into a speed or a printed formula, symbol by symbol, and keep the display.
Round a greatest count of whole items down.
Meet the twists: hours and minutes, a formula to rearrange, Pythagoras.

A bounds item in 14 of the 15 M4 papers since 2018, usually at Q12 to Q17. Two or three marks when the bounds go straight into a calculation; four when a second stage comes first: hours and minutes, a count or Pythagoras. The first mark is for the bounds; the last is the value, as the full display unless an accuracy is named. Stuck: write every half unit and all four bounds.

workedExamples.stem:
A shelf has an internal width of $96$ cm, correct to the nearest centimetre. A row of box files standing on it has a total width of $91.5$ cm, correct to the nearest $0.5$ cm.

Find the greatest possible gap left on the shelf, and the least possible gap.

steps.working: Shelf: half unit $= 0.5$, so $95.5 \le w < 96.5$. Files: half unit $= 0.25$, so $91.25 \le f < 91.75$.
steps.decision: The half unit is half of the rounding unit, and the rounding unit is whatever the question names. Nearest centimetre halves to 0.5; nearest 0.5 cm halves to 0.25. I write all four bounds before I write anything else, because every later choice is a choice between them.

options: 0.25, because the rounding unit is 0.5 cm and half of 0.5 is 0.25
0.5, because measurements are always bounded by half a centimetre
0.05, because 91.5 is given to one decimal place
whyMenu.explain: The stem names the rounding unit, not the number of decimal places. Nearest 0.5 cm gives a half unit of 0.25 cm.

steps.decision: I write the calculation in symbols first. The gap is a subtraction, so the two quantities pull in opposite directions: whatever makes the shelf larger makes the gap larger, and whatever makes the files larger makes the gap smaller.
Widest possible shelf, narrowest possible files: upper bound minus lower bound. In November 2025 some candidates used two upper bounds here instead.
The mirror image: narrowest shelf, widest files. Lower bound minus upper bound. Neither answer uses 96 or 91.5 anywhere.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Greatest gap $5.25$ cm, least gap $3.75$ cm

twin.stem: A doorway is $78$ cm wide, correct to the nearest centimetre. A wardrobe is $76.5$ cm wide, correct to the nearest $0.5$ cm. Find the greatest possible clearance when the wardrobe is carried through.

workedExamples.stem:
A sandbag has a mass of $35$ kg, correct to the nearest $5$ kg. The safe working load of a hoist is $900$ kg, correct to the nearest $50$ kg.

Work out the greatest possible number of sandbags the hoist can lift.

steps.decision: Half of 5 is 2.5. Summer 2025 was lost on this line: for a mass to the nearest 5 kg, more candidates took off the whole 5 than half of it. Anything from 32.5 kg up to 37.5 kg rounds to 35 kg, so 32.5 is the lower bound.

options: 32.5 kg, because half of 5 kg is 2.5 kg
30 kg, because the next multiple of 5 below 35 is 30
34.5 kg, because 35 is a whole number so the half unit is 0.5
whyMenu.explain: Anything from 32.5 kg up to 37.5 kg rounds to 35 kg when you round to the nearest 5 kg, so 32.5 is the lower bound.

steps.decision: Half of 50 is 25. Same rule, larger unit; nothing about the method changes.

steps.working: Number of bags $=$ load $\div$ mass of one bag, so greatest $= 925 \div 32.5$
steps.decision: A division, so the pairing is an upper over a lower. Heaviest possible allowance, lightest possible bag: both push the count up.
I keep the display. Rounding here to 28.5 or 28.46 is the slip the November 2025 report warns against.

A count of bags is a whole number, and 29 bags would weigh at least $29 \times 32.5 = 942.5$ kg, which is more than 925 kg. So the decimal is rounded down, not up: 28 bags weigh at least 910 kg, which the hoist can take.

options: 28, because 29 bags would need at least 942.5 kg of allowance
28.5, because the answer should be given to one decimal place
whyMenu.explain: A greatest possible count is rounded down: the 29th bag does not fit under any allowed load. Leaving a decimal scores nothing for the final mark.

twin.stem: A paving slab has a mass of $18$ kg, correct to the nearest $2$ kg. A trolley is rated to carry $260$ kg, correct to the nearest $20$ kg. Work out the greatest possible number of slabs the trolley can carry.

workedExamples.stem:
A train travels $87$ km, correct to the nearest kilometre. The journey takes $1$ hour $24$ minutes, correct to the nearest minute.

Calculate the maximum average speed of the train in km/h.

steps.working: Distance: $86.5 \le d < 87.5$, so the upper bound is $87.5$ km.
steps.decision: Nearest kilometre, half unit 0.5. Speed is distance divided by time, so the largest speed wants the largest distance.

steps.working: $1$ h $24$ min $= 84$ minutes, so $83.5 \le t < 84.5$ minutes.
steps.decision: I turn the time into one unit before I bound it. The accuracy is to the nearest minute, so the half unit is half a minute — and it is half a minute of the total, 84 minutes, not of the 24.

steps.working: Minimum time $= 83.5 \div 60 = 1.391666\ldots$ h, keeping the display.
steps.decision: km/h needs hours. Minutes divided by 60 gives decimal hours. Writing 1 h 23.5 min as 1.235 h is the slip the Summer 2023 report singled out, and it is not a small one: it changes this answer by about 8 km/h.

options: $1.235$ h, because 1 h 23.5 min reads as 1.235
$1.235$ h, because 23.5 minutes is 0.235 of an hour
whyMenu.explain: Minutes are sixtieths, not hundredths or thousandths. Divide the whole time in minutes by 60.

steps.decision: Largest distance over smallest time. I use the stored value, not 1.42, so the display is the answer the scheme prints. Equivalently $87.5 \times 60 \div 83.5$.

twin.stem: A ferry crosses $54$ km, correct to the nearest kilometre, in $2$ hours $18$ minutes, correct to the nearest minute. Calculate the maximum average speed in km/h.

workedExamples.stem:
A ball bearing rolls down a ramp and stops after a distance $s$ metres, where

$s = \dfrac{v^2}{2a}$

$v = 5.82$ m/s, correct to $3$ significant figures.
$a = 3.6$ m/s$^2$, correct to $1$ decimal place.

Using those bounds, calculate the upper bound of $s$. Leave the full calculator display.

steps.working: $v$: last significant figure is the hundredths, half unit $0.005$, so $5.815 \le v < 5.825$.
steps.decision: Three significant figures in 5.82 means the 2 is the last one, in the hundredths column, so the half unit is 0.005. Significant figures are counted from the first non-zero digit, and the half unit belongs to the place value of the last one.

steps.working: $a$: one decimal place, half unit $0.05$, so $3.55 \le a < 3.65$.
steps.decision: Half of 0.1 is 0.05. All four bounds are now on the page.

steps.working: $s$ largest when $v$ is largest and $a$ is smallest: $s_{\max} = \dfrac{5.825^2}{2 \times 3.55}$
steps.decision: $v$ is on the top, so the biggest $v$ gives the biggest $s$. $a$ is on the bottom, so the smallest $a$ gives the biggest $s$. The formula is read symbol by symbol: $v$ is squared and $a$ is doubled. The Summer 2024 and November 2024 reports both name the formula slips: the top letter not squared, the bottom one not doubled.

options: $\dfrac{5.825^2}{3.55}$, because the 2 belongs to the square
$\dfrac{5.825}{2 \times 3.55}$, because the square applies to the whole fraction
whyMenu.explain: The 2 multiplies $a$ and the square sits on $v$ only. Both slips are named in the November 2024 report.

steps.decision: I write both intermediate values in full. No rounding: 33.93 and 7.1 would already cost accuracy in the final figure.
The display is the answer. Substituting the given values would have produced 4.7045, which is not an upper bound of anything.

twin.stem: For the same formula $s = \dfrac{v^2}{2a}$, take $v = 7.64$ m/s correct to $3$ significant figures and $a = 2.5$ m/s$^2$ correct to $1$ decimal place. Using those bounds, calculate the upper bound of $s$.

items.stem: A crate has a mass of $60$ kg, correct to the nearest $5$ kg. What is the lower bound of its mass?
items.skill: Half unit for a rounding unit larger than 1

options.feedback: Half of 5 is 2.5, so anything from 57.5 kg up to 62.5 kg rounds to 60 kg. The lower bound is 57.5 kg.
The whole 5 was subtracted instead of half of it. A mass of 56 kg would round to 55 kg, not 60 kg, so 55 is too low. Summer 2025 M4 Q13 turned on exactly this line.
That is the half unit for the nearest whole kilogram. The stem says nearest 5 kg, so halve the 5, not the 1.

items.stem: A length is $9.47$ cm, correct to $3$ significant figures. What is its upper bound?

options.feedback: The third significant figure, 7, is in the hundredths, so the half unit is 0.005: 9.47 + 0.005 = 9.475 cm.
A whole unit of the last place was added. The bound sits half a unit away: 9.475 cm.
That treats the length as 2 significant figures. 9, 4 and 7 are three, so the half unit is 0.005.

items.stem: A rope is $250$ m long, correct to the nearest $10$ m. What is its lower bound?
items.skill: Half unit from a rounding unit

options.feedback: Half of 10 m is 5 m, so the lower bound is 250 − 5 = 245 m.
The whole 10 m was taken off. The switch to 240 happens halfway, at 245 m.
That halves 1 m, but the rope is to the nearest 10 m: half of 10 is 5, so 245 m.

items.stem: $a = 9.2$ correct to $1$ decimal place and $b = 3.74$ correct to $2$ decimal places. What is the greatest possible value of $a - b$?

options.feedback: Upper bound of $a$ minus lower bound of $b$: $9.25 - 3.735 = 5.515$. Take the most and remove the least.
Both upper bounds were used: $9.25 - 3.745$. Subtracting a larger number makes the answer smaller, so this is not the maximum.
That is $9.2 - 3.74$, the given values. A bounds question never uses them; they are the middle of each interval.

items.stem: $p = 63$ correct to the nearest whole number and $q = 4.8$ correct to $1$ decimal place. What is the greatest possible value of $p \div q$, to $3$ decimal places?

options.feedback: $63.5 \div 4.75 = 13.368\ldots$: the biggest top over the smallest bottom.
Both upper bounds were used: $63.5 \div 4.85$. Dividing by a larger number makes the answer smaller, so this is below the maximum.
That is $63 \div 4.8$, the given values. The bounds go in before you divide.

items.stem: A journey takes $1$ hour $36$ minutes, correct to the nearest minute. What is the shortest possible time, in hours?
items.skill: Bounding a time given in hours and minutes

options.feedback: $1$ h $36$ min $= 96$ min, so the lower bound is $95.5$ min, and $95.5 \div 60 = 1.591666\ldots$ h.
1 h 35.5 min has been read as the decimal 1.355. Minutes are sixtieths: change the whole time to minutes, bound it, then divide by 60. Summer 2023 M4 Q15 was lost here.
That is the given time, $96 \div 60$, with no bound applied. The shortest possible time is half a minute less.

items.stem: You are asked for the upper bound of a calculation. What do you do first?
items.skill: Bound the inputs, not the answer

options.text: Replace each given value by the bound that makes the result largest, then calculate once.
options.feedback: Bounds go in at the start. One substitution, one calculation, and the display is the bound. Full-mark answers in November 2025 listed all four bounds first.

options.text: Calculate with the given values, then add half a unit to the answer.
options.feedback: Half units do not survive a calculation: squaring, dividing and square-rooting all change them. About 30% reached full marks on November 2025 M4 Q17 and this was the main reason.

options.text: Calculate with the given values, then round the answer up.
options.feedback: Rounding up is not the same as an upper bound. The upper bound comes from the inputs, and it is usually nowhere near the rounded-up value.

items.stem: A length has lower bound $6.0473\ldots$ m and upper bound $6.0518\ldots$ m. What is the length to a suitable degree of accuracy?
items.skill: Choosing a degree of accuracy from the bounds

options.feedback: Round both bounds: to 3 significant figures both give 6.05, so 6.05 m is safe. To 4 significant figures they give 6.047 and 6.052, which disagree, so stop at three.
Only the lower bound was rounded. The upper bound gives 6.052 to the same accuracy, so the fourth figure is not known and cannot be quoted.
A midpoint is a guess dressed up as precision. A suitable degree of accuracy is the figures on which the two bounds actually agree.

items.stem: A greatest possible number of jars works out as $52.81$. What goes on the answer line?

options.feedback: A 53rd jar would go over even the largest allowed load, so a greatest count rounds down: 52.
Rounding up adds a jar that cannot fit under any allowed total. Round a greatest count down.
Only whole jars count, so a decimal is not a possible number. Round down to 52.

context.setting: Pure number, no context

parts.stem:
$a = 14.7$ correct to $1$ decimal place and $b = 8.24$ correct to $2$ decimal places.

context.setting: A lorry's day-long delivery run

parts.stem:
A lorry covers $315$ km, correct to the **nearest 5 km**, in $4.2$ hours, correct to $1$ decimal place.

Calculate the maximum possible average speed of the lorry.

Give your answer to $3$ **significant figures**.

scheme.for: 76.5, from 76.50602410; the full display is also accepted

hints: Half of 5 km is 2.5 km; half of 0.1 h is 0.05 h.
Speed = distance ÷ time, so the maximum wants the furthest distance in the shortest time.
The stem states 3 significant figures, so round once, at the very end.
parts.workedSolution: Distance: $312.5 \le d < 317.5$. Time: $4.15 \le t < 4.25$. Maximum speed $= 317.5 \div 4.15 = 76.50602409\ldots$ km/h, which is $76.5$ km/h to $3$ significant figures.

context.setting: A projectile formula used in a physics class

parts.stem:
The greatest height $h$ metres reached by a ball thrown straight up is given by

$h = \dfrac{u^2}{2g}$

$u = 13.7$ m/s, correct to $1$ decimal place.
$g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$, correct to $1$ decimal place.

Using those bounds, calculate the **upper bound** of $h$.
hints: $u$ is on the top, so the largest $u$ gives the largest $h$; $g$ is on the bottom, so the smallest $g$ gives the largest $h$.
Square the bound of $u$ and double the bound of $g$.

commonErrors.feedback: $g$ was not doubled: the calculation was $13.75^2 \div 9.75$. The 2 multiplies $g$, and the bounds were already right, so this is a reading error, not a bounds error. Summer 2024 and November 2024 both name it.
The given values 13.7 and 9.8 were substituted. That is the value of $h$ itself, not its upper bound: the bounds must go in before the calculation.

context.setting: A right-angled triangle with two measured sides

parts.stem:
In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is $12.8$ cm, correct to $1$ decimal place, and one of the shorter sides is $7.35$ cm, correct to $2$ decimal places.

Calculate the **upper bound** of the third side.
hints: Pythagoras' theorem is not on the formula sheet: $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, so the third side is $\sqrt{c^2 - a^2}$.
Under the square root there is a subtraction, so pair the largest hypotenuse with the smallest known side.

commonErrors.feedback: Both upper bounds went under the root. The known side is being taken away, so the smallest one leaves the most: pair 12.85 with 7.345. November 2025 M4 Q17 turned on this pairing.
The third side was found from the given values and then half a unit was added. Half units do not pass through a square root; bound the two sides first, then calculate once.

context.setting: A right-angled triangle LMN with two measured sides

figures.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 340 235' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Right-angled triangle LMN with the right angle at M, hypotenuse LN marked 9.36 cm and side LM marked 6.2 cm'><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'><path d='M60 40 L60 180 L290 180 Z'/><path d='M60 161 L79 161 L79 180'/></g><g font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor'><text x='44' y='33'>L</text><text x='42' y='201'>M</text><text x='294' y='201'>N</text><text x='4' y='116'>6.2 cm</text><text x='188' y='98'>9.36 cm</text><text x='60' y='228' font-size='14'>diagram not drawn accurately</text></g></svg>

parts.stem:
In triangle $LMN$ the angle at $M$ is a right angle.

$LN = 9.36$ cm, correct to $3$ significant figures.
$LM = 6.2$ cm, correct to $1$ decimal place.

Write down the bound of $LN$ and the bound of $LM$ that make $MN$ as large as possible.
hints: Three significant figures in 9.36 puts the last one in the hundredths, so the half unit is 0.005.
$MN^2 = LN^2 - LM^2$, and $LM$ is the one being taken away.
parts.workedSolution: $LN$: half unit $0.005$, so the upper bound is $9.365$ cm. $LM$: half unit $0.05$, so the lower bound is $6.15$ cm. $MN$ is largest when the hypotenuse is largest and the side removed is smallest.

commonErrors.feedback: The upper bound of $LM$ was chosen. Inside $LN^2 - LM^2$ the term $LM^2$ is subtracted, so a smaller $LM$ leaves a bigger answer. This is the pairing November 2025 candidates reversed.

parts.stem:
Calculate the upper bound of $MN$.

Leave the **full calculator display**.

scheme.for: 7.062628760 (the full display; accept 7.06 only if an accuracy had been stated)

hints: $MN = \sqrt{LN^2 - LM^2}$.
Square each bound before you subtract.
parts.workedSolution: $$MN_{\max} = \sqrt{9.365^2 - 6.15^2} = \sqrt{87.703225 - 37.8225} = \sqrt{49.880725} = 7.062628759\ldots$$ cm. Nothing is rounded on the way, and the display is what goes on the answer line.

commonErrors.feedback: $MN$ was found from $9.36$ and $6.2$ first and half a unit was added afterwards. Squaring and square-rooting do not carry a half unit through; about 30% of candidates reached full marks in November 2025 and this was the main loss.
The bound was rounded with no accuracy asked for. The scheme prints the long value, so leave the display; a rounded figure risks the accuracy mark.

parts.stem: Explain why the lower bound of $LM$, and not its upper bound, is used in part (b).

accepted: MN squared is LN squared minus LM squared, so taking away a smaller LM leaves a larger MN.
LM is subtracted, so the smallest LM gives the greatest MN.

reject: because lower bounds are always used

scheme.for: states that LM squared is subtracted, so a smaller LM leaves a larger MN
accept: it is being taken away so the least value leaves the most
reject: because it is the lower bound

hints: Look at where $LM$ sits in $LN^2 - LM^2$.
Say what taking away less does to the answer.
parts.workedSolution: $MN^2 = LN^2 - LM^2$, so $LM^2$ is subtracted. Taking away as little as possible leaves as much as possible, which is why $MN$ is largest when $LM$ is at its lower bound.

commonErrors.feedback: Naming the bound is not a reason. The mark is for saying that $LM^2$ is subtracted, so the smallest $LM$ leaves the largest $MN$.

context.setting: A cyclist's timed ride between two towns

parts.stem:
A cyclist rides $41$ km, correct to the nearest kilometre. The ride takes $1$ hour $52$ minutes, correct to the nearest minute.

Work out the **shortest possible** time for the ride, in hours.

scheme.for: 112 minutes seen and 111.5 as the lower bound

hints: Turn the whole time into minutes first: $1$ h $52$ min $= 112$ min.
Nearest minute, so the half unit is half a minute.
Divide by 60 to get decimal hours.
parts.workedSolution: $1$ h $52$ min $= 112$ minutes, so $111.5 \le t < 112.5$ minutes. In hours the shortest possible time is $111.5 \div 60 = 1.858333333\ldots$ h.

commonErrors.feedback: $1$ h $51.5$ min has been written as the decimal $1.515$. Minutes are sixtieths of an hour, so convert the whole time to minutes, bound it, then divide by 60. Summer 2023 M4 Q15 was lost on this line.
111.5 is the time in minutes. The part asks for hours, and part (b) needs hours because the speed is in km/h.

parts.stem: Calculate the **greatest possible** average speed of the cyclist, in km/h.

scheme.for: 41.5 identified as the upper bound of the distance
41.5 divided by their shortest time in hours, or 41.5 × 60 ÷ 111.5

hints: Speed $=$ distance $\div$ time; it is not on the formula sheet.
Greatest speed: furthest distance in the shortest time.
parts.workedSolution: Distance: $40.5 \le d < 41.5$. Greatest average speed $= 41.5 \div 1.858333333\ldots = 22.331838565\ldots$ km/h. Equivalently $41.5 \times 60 \div 111.5$. The stored value is used, not $1.86$.

commonErrors.feedback: The time was rounded to 1.86 h before dividing. Keep the stored value: the scheme prints the long answer and rounding part-way moves the third figure.
$41 \div (112 \div 60)$ uses the given values, so it is the average speed itself and not a greatest possible value.

context.setting: A metal block weighed and measured in a workshop

parts.stem:
A metal block has a mass of $248$ g, correct to the nearest gram, and a volume of $92$ cm$^3$, correct to the nearest cm$^3$.

Write down the upper and lower bounds of the mass and of the volume.
hints: Nearest gram: half unit 0.5 g.
Nearest cm³: half unit 0.5 cm³.

parts.stem:
Density $=$ mass $\div$ volume.

Calculate the upper and lower bounds of the density of the block, in g/cm$^3$.

scheme.for: 2.715846995 and 2.675675676 (accept the full displays or 2.7158 and 2.6757)

hints: The largest density is the largest mass in the smallest volume.
The smallest density is the smallest mass in the largest volume.

commonErrors.feedback: $248.5 \div 92.5$ uses both upper bounds, so it is neither bound of the density. On the bottom of a fraction, the smallest value gives the largest result.

parts.stem:
Write down the density of the block to a **suitable degree of accuracy**.

Explain how your two bounds justify the accuracy you have chosen.

accepted: 2.7 g/cm3 because both bounds round to 2.7 to 2 significant figures, and to 3 significant figures they give 2.72 and 2.68, which disagree.
2.7 g/cm3; the bounds agree to 2 significant figures only.

scheme.for: reason: both bounds round to 2.7 to 2 significant figures, and they differ at 3 significant figures

hints: Round both bounds to 1, then 2, then 3 significant figures and watch where they stop agreeing.
Quote the last accuracy at which they still agree.

context.setting: Crates loaded onto a trailer at a builders' yard

parts.stem:
Each crate has a mass of $24$ kg, correct to the **nearest 2 kg**.

A trailer can carry a load of $700$ kg, correct to the **nearest 20 kg**.

Work out the **greatest possible number** of crates the trailer can carry.

Show your working clearly.

scheme.examinerNote: A maximum count is rounded down and must be a whole number.

hints: Half of 2 kg is 1 kg; half of 20 kg is 10 kg.
The most crates fit when the allowance is largest and each crate is lightest.
$710 \div 23 = 30.8695\ldots$, and a crate cannot be a fraction.
parts.workedSolution: Crate: $23 \le m < 25$. Trailer: $690 \le L < 710$. Greatest number $= 710 \div 23 = 30.869565\ldots$ Crates are whole, and $31$ crates would weigh at least $31 \times 23 = 713$ kg, which is above $710$ kg. So the greatest possible number is $30$.

commonErrors.feedback: The whole rounding units were added and subtracted: $720 \div 22$. Halve the rounding unit — 1 kg for the crate, 10 kg for the trailer. Summer 2025 M4 Q13 was decided on exactly this.
$30.87$ was rounded up. The 31st crate does not fit under any allowed load, so a greatest possible count is always rounded down; leaving 30.87 also loses the final mark.
$700 \div 24$ uses the given values. The bounds have to be written down before the division; those are the first two marks.

A circle of radius $5.4$ cm is cut from a rectangular sheet of card measuring $24.6$ cm by $18.3$ cm.

Each measurement is correct to $1$ decimal place.

Write down the three bounds needed to make the area of card left as large as possible.
hints: Every measurement has a half unit of 0.05.
A bigger rectangle leaves more card; a bigger hole leaves less.
parts.workedSolution: The rectangle takes both upper bounds, $24.65$ cm and $18.35$ cm, because a larger rectangle leaves more card. The circle takes its lower bound, $5.35$ cm, because a smaller hole removes less.

commonErrors.feedback: The circle was given its upper bound too. It is being removed, so the biggest area left needs the smallest possible circle.

parts.stem:
Calculate the **greatest possible** area of card left after the circle has been cut out.

Give your answer to $1$ decimal place.

scheme.for: their rectangle area - their circle area
362.4 (from 362.4072643); accept 362.41 or the full display only if 1 d.p. is also given

hints: Area of a circle is $\pi r^2$ and it is not on the formula sheet.
Use the stored value of $\pi$, not $3.14$.

commonErrors.feedback: The given values were used: $24.6 \times 18.3 - \pi \times 5.4^2$. That is the area itself, not its greatest possible value. The first two marks are for the bounded areas.

context.setting: A sample of brass weighed and measured in a laboratory

parts.stem:
A sample of brass has a mass of $57.2$ g, correct to $1$ decimal place, and a volume of $6.8$ cm$^3$, correct to $1$ decimal place.

Calculate the minimum possible density of the brass.
hints: Density = mass ÷ volume, and it is not on the formula sheet.
The smallest density comes from the smallest mass in the largest volume.

commonErrors.feedback: $57.25 \div 6.85$ uses both upper bounds. A larger mass makes the density larger, so the minimum needs the smallest mass over the largest volume: $57.15 \div 6.85$.
$57.2 \div 6.8$ uses the given values, so it is the density itself, not its least possible value. Write the bounds first, then divide.

context.setting: A square cut from a rectangle of sheet metal

parts.stem:
A rectangle of sheet metal measures $21.4$ cm by $13.8$ cm, each correct to $1$ decimal place. A square of side $5.6$ cm, correct to $1$ decimal place, is cut out of it.

Calculate the **greatest possible** area of metal left.

scheme.for: their rectangle area − their square area

hints: The area left is a subtraction, so the rectangle wants to be as large as possible and the square as small as possible.
Upper bounds of both sides of the rectangle; lower bound of the side of the square.
parts.workedSolution: Greatest area left $= 21.45 \times 13.85 - 5.55^2$. The rectangle is $297.0825$ and the square $30.8025$, so the greatest area left is $297.0825 - 30.8025 = 266.28$ cm$^2$. Both sides of the rectangle take their upper bound because its area is a product; the square takes its lower bound because it is removed.

commonErrors.feedback: The square was given its upper bound as well: $297.0825 - 5.65^2$. A larger hole leaves less metal, so the greatest area left needs the smallest square.
$21.4 \times 13.8 - 5.6^2$ uses the given values, so it is the area left itself, not its greatest possible value. Bound every length first.

context.setting: A ladder leaning against a vertical wall

parts.stem:
A ladder $6.4$ m long, correct to $1$ decimal place, leans against a vertical wall on level ground. Its foot is $1.85$ m from the wall, correct to $2$ decimal places.

Calculate the **least possible** height the top of the ladder reaches up the wall. Give your answer correct to $3$ decimal places.
hints: The height squared is the ladder squared minus the distance squared: a subtraction.
Least height: the shortest ladder, and take away the largest distance.
parts.workedSolution: Height$^2 =$ ladder$^2 -$ distance$^2$, so the least height takes the lower bound of the ladder, $6.35$, and the upper bound of the distance, $1.855$. $6.35^2 - 1.855^2 = 36.881475$, and $\sqrt{36.881475} = 6.07301202\ldots$, so the least height is $6.073$ m to $3$ decimal places.

commonErrors.feedback: Both lower bounds were used: $\sqrt{6.35^2 - 1.845^2}$. Taking away a smaller distance leaves more, so for the least height take away the largest distance, $1.855$.
$\sqrt{6.4^2 - 1.85^2}$ uses the given values, so it is the height itself, not its least possible value. Bound the ladder and the distance first.

context.setting: A drone flight across a field

parts.stem:
A drone flies in a straight line from $P$ to $Q$. $Q$ is $1.84$ km east and $2.65$ km north of $P$, each distance correct to $2$ decimal places. The flight takes $4$ minutes $30$ seconds, correct to the nearest $10$ seconds.

Write down the upper bound of the distance east and the upper bound of the distance north.
hints: Two decimal places: the half unit is 0.005.
Upper bound = stated value + half unit.
parts.workedSolution: Two decimal places means the nearest $0.01$, so the half unit is $0.005$: east $1.845$ km and north $2.655$ km.

parts.stem: Calculate the upper bound of the distance $PQ$. Leave the full calculator display.

scheme.for: 3.23311769 (the square root of their sum; the full display)

hints: PQ is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with the two distances as its shorter sides.
A sum of squares: both distances at their upper bounds give the longest PQ.
parts.workedSolution: $PQ^2 = 1.845^2 + 2.655^2 = 10.45305$, so the upper bound of $PQ$ is $\sqrt{10.45305} = 3.23311769\ldots$ km. The two squares are added, so both distances take their upper bounds, as in a sum.

commonErrors.feedback: $\sqrt{1.84^2 + 2.65^2}$ uses the given values, so it is $PQ$ itself, not its upper bound.
$PQ$ was found from $1.84$ and $2.65$ and half a unit added afterwards. A half unit does not survive squaring and a square root: bound the two distances first.
The display was rounded with no accuracy asked for. The scheme prints the long value: leave $3.23311769$.

parts.stem: Work out the shortest possible time of the flight, in hours.

scheme.for: 270 seconds and 265 as its lower bound

hints: Change the whole time to seconds first: 4 minutes 30 seconds is 270 seconds.
Nearest 10 seconds: the half unit is 5 seconds.
3600 seconds make an hour.

commonErrors.feedback: 0.075 h is 4 minutes 30 seconds itself. The shortest time is 5 seconds less: 265 seconds, then divide by 3600.
4 min 25 s was written as 4.25 minutes, but seconds are sixtieths of a minute. Change the whole time to seconds first: 265 seconds.

parts.stem: Hence calculate the greatest possible average speed of the drone, in km/h. Give your answer correct to $1$ decimal place.

scheme.for: their upper bound of PQ ÷ their shortest time

hints: Speed = distance ÷ time.
Greatest speed: the longest distance over the shortest time.
Use the stored values, not rounded ones.
parts.workedSolution: Greatest speed $= 3.23311769\ldots \div 0.07361111111\ldots$, which is $43.92159881\ldots$, so $43.9$ km/h to $1$ decimal place.

commonErrors.feedback: The time took its upper bound as well: dividing by $275$ seconds gives a smaller speed. The greatest speed needs the shortest time, $265$ seconds.

context.setting: Fencing round a rectangular garden

parts.stem:
A rectangular garden is $14.6$ m long, correct to $1$ decimal place, and $9.25$ m wide, correct to $2$ decimal places.

Work out the **least possible** perimeter of the garden.
hints: A perimeter is a sum, so nothing is taken away.
The least sum uses both lower bounds.

commonErrors.feedback: $2(14.6 + 9.25)$ uses the given values, so it is the perimeter itself, not its least possible value. A sum takes both lower bounds.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh was asked: a sack of feed weighs $20$ kg, correct to the nearest $5$ kg; a store can hold $600$ kg, correct to the nearest $50$ kg. Work out the greatest possible number of sacks the store can hold. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The whole rounding unit was added and subtracted instead of half of it. Correct to the nearest 5 kg means the half unit is 2.5 kg, so the bounds are 17.5 kg and 22.5 kg. Line 2 has the same slip: half of 50 is 25, so the store bounds are 575 kg and 625 kg.
correction: Sack: 17.5 kg to 22.5 kg (half of 5 is 2.5)
Store: 575 kg to 625 kg (half of 50 is 25)
So 35 sacks, because 36 sacks would weigh at least 36 x 17.5 = 630 kg
findTheMistake.feedback: The structure is right: bounds first, then largest allowance divided by lightest sack, which is worth the method mark. Both bound lines use the whole rounding unit, and the last line then rounds a maximum count up. Halve the rounding unit, and round a greatest possible count down. Summer 2025 M4 Q13 lost most of its marks in exactly these two places.

findTheMistake.stem: Eoin was asked: in a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is $8.42$ cm, correct to $3$ significant figures, and one shorter side is $5.3$ cm, correct to $1$ decimal place. Using those bounds, calculate the upper bound of the third side. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The third side was calculated from the given values and the bound was added to the answer afterwards. Squaring and square-rooting change the size of a half unit, so a half unit added at the end means nothing. The bounds belong in line 1, and the correct pairing is the upper bound of the hypotenuse with the lower bound of the known side.
correction: Upper bound of the third side = sqrt(43.418125) = 6.589243128
findTheMistake.feedback: Pythagoras was set up correctly, but no mark is available until the bounds go in, so this scores nothing. Write the four bounds first, choose the upper hypotenuse with the lower side because that side is being taken away, then calculate once and leave the display. November 2025 M4 Q17: about 30% reached full marks, and bounding the answer instead of the inputs was the main reason.

findTheMistake.stem: Saoirse was asked: a runner covers $18$ km, correct to the nearest kilometre, in a time of $1$ hour $17$ minutes, correct to the nearest minute. Work out the greatest possible average speed, in km/h. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: 1 hour 16.5 minutes was written as the decimal 1.165 hours. Minutes are sixtieths of an hour, not thousandths. The time should be turned into minutes first: 1 h 17 min is 77 minutes, so the minimum is 76.5 minutes, and 76.5 divided by 60 is 1.275 hours.
correction: 1 h 17 min = 77 minutes, so the minimum time is 76.5 minutes
Leave the full display unless an accuracy is stated
findTheMistake.feedback: The distance bound and the shape of the calculation are right, which earns the first method mark. The time conversion is the whole question: minutes divided by 60 gives decimal hours, and the error here moves the answer by about 1.4 km/h. Summer 2023 M4 Q15 was one of the least-answered questions on the paper for this reason, and rounding the final display to 15.9 would risk the accuracy mark as well.

findings.asked: Use bounds of a distance and a time (in hours and minutes) to find a maximum average speed.

findings.rule: Convert minutes to hours by dividing by 60 before finding bounds; max speed = max distance / min time.

findings.asked: Substitute bounds into a formula of the form v squared = u squared + 2as.
findings.wentWrong: Bounds were mostly identified. Errors were in the formula itself (u not squared, a not doubled); the weakest just substituted the given values.
findings.rule: Write the four bounds, then substitute the combination that maximises the target, using the formula exactly.

findings.asked: Bounds in a formula to find a maximum value.
findings.wentWrong: Improving year on year; the same formula slips (V not squared, g not doubled) and rounding errors at the end.
findings.rule: Read the formula symbol by symbol; keep the full display.

findings.asked: Maximum number of items given a total mass to the nearest 100 kg and an item mass to the nearest 5 kg.
findings.wentWrong: The nearest-5 bound was the problem: 45 was used instead of 47.5. Many did get the upper bound 1550. Some did not give a whole number, or rounded up when a maximum count must round down.
findings.rule: Half of 5 is 2.5; a maximum number of whole items is rounded down.

findings.wentWrong: About 30% got full marks. Many calculated with the given values and then bounded the answer; some used both upper bounds where the subtraction needed one upper and one lower; most rounded the result (3.86) instead of leaving the whole display.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Listed all four bounds, chose upper hypotenuse with lower leg for the maximum, and left the full display as the bound.
findings.rule: Bound the inputs, not the output; in a subtraction pair the biggest with the smallest.

insight.ruleToRemember: Write all four bounds first; subtraction and division mix an upper with a lower; convert units (minutes to decimal hours) before bounding; keep the full calculator display for a bound and round a maximum count down.
insight.aStarSignal: Bounds threaded through a two-stage calculation (a formula or Pythagoras, or a speed with a time in hours and minutes) with the right max/min pairing at each stage.
